skill.work: I'm a bit apprehensive about tomorrow's review with the client.
skill.everyday: She was apprehensive before her first drive on the highway.
skill.analogy: Like the quiet moment before the exam paper is handed out.
skill.insteadOf: I am having some tension about tomorrow.

meaning: Anxious or fearful that something bad or unpleasant will happen soon.
contrast: Not panic or terror; it is a quiet, anticipatory dread before an uncertain outcome.
example: I felt apprehensive walking into the quarterly board review after our infrastructure migration slipped.

skill.work: When the load test passed, Arjun felt vindicated about his design.
skill.everyday: The shortcut I suggested really was faster — I felt vindicated.
skill.analogy: Like a DRS review proving the batsman was right to challenge.
skill.insteadOf: I felt happy that I was proved correct.

meaning: Feeling cleared of blame or proven right after being doubted.
contrast: Not gloating or petty; it is the quiet relief of objective reality confirming your original conviction.
example: When the stress test passed under 100k concurrent users, the caching team felt completely vindicated.

skill.work: After the third meeting on the same issue, Priya was exasperated.
skill.everyday: I was exasperated when the fourth auto driver refused to go.
skill.analogy: Like a pressure cooker on its third whistle: patience is gone.
skill.insteadOf: I was very, very irritated.

meaning: Intensely irritated, frustrated, and fatigued by repeated friction.
contrast: Beyond standard annoyance; you have tried multiple solutions and are out of patience.
example: After the third meeting where we relitigated the same resolved API spec, she was visibly exasperated.

skill.work: I'm ambivalent about the new role: more reach, less hands-on work.
skill.everyday: I'm ambivalent about moving cities: a better job, but far from family.
skill.analogy: Like standing between two trains, wanting to board both.
skill.insteadOf: I am confused, I like it and I don't like it.

meaning: Having simultaneous conflicting feelings or contradictory attitudes about something.
contrast: Not apathy (not caring); it is caring strongly in two opposing directions at once.
example: I'm ambivalent about taking the manager track—I love team coaching, but I'll miss hands-on architecture.

skill.work: Three good quarters made us complacent about testing.
skill.everyday: He got complacent after clearing the first round and stopped practising.
skill.analogy: Like a team at 200 for 1 that stops running hard between wickets.
skill.insteadOf: We became too relaxed because things were going well.

meaning: Smug self-satisfaction accompanied by an unawareness of impending danger or competition.
contrast: Different from confident; confidence is grounded in rigor, complacency is blinded by past wins.
example: Dominating the market for three years made leadership complacent about mobile UX innovation.

skill.work: The team felt demoralized when the project was cancelled a week before launch.
skill.everyday: After five losses in a row, the colony cricket team was demoralized.
skill.analogy: Like a team walking off after a heavy defeat, heads down.
skill.insteadOf: Everyone lost their energy and interest.

meaning: Having lost confidence, hope, or enthusiasm after repeated setbacks.
contrast: Deeper than tired; your internal belief in the project's eventual success has eroded.
example: Canceling the product line two weeks before release left the engineering squad deeply demoralized.

skill.work: Despite the tight deadline, the team stayed upbeat all week.
skill.everyday: Even after missing the flight, Dad was in good spirits and joking.
skill.analogy: Like a cork in water: push it down and it pops right back up.
skill.insteadOf: The team stayed buoyant all week.

meaning: Cheerful, resilient, and optimistically energetic despite headwinds.
contrast: You'll mostly see it in writing. In speech, most people say "upbeat" or "in good spirits".
example: Despite the tight deadline, the design team maintained a buoyant, collaborative mood.

skill.work: I'm wary of promising a date before we've tested it.
skill.everyday: Be wary of anyone on WhatsApp asking for an OTP.
skill.analogy: Like crossing a busy road: you look both ways before stepping out.
skill.insteadOf: I am a little scared to commit.

meaning: Feeling or showing keen caution about possible dangers or hidden traps.
contrast: Not cowardice; it is calculated, tactical vigilance before committing resources.
example: Senior engineers were wary of adopting the unproven database framework for primary billing.

skill.work: After a year of ignored suggestions, he felt disillusioned with the team.
skill.everyday: He felt disillusioned when his dream city turned out noisy and lonely.
skill.analogy: Like finding out the famous restaurant uses packet masala.
skill.insteadOf: I lost my trust and interest in it.

meaning: Disappointed upon discovering that something is not as good, honest, or noble as once believed.
contrast: Beyond temporary sadness; it is the erosion of an earlier idealistic belief.
example: After seeing leadership ignore systemic security findings for a year, senior engineers felt deeply disillusioned.

skill.work: The client's sharp questions rattled her for a moment, but she recovered.
skill.everyday: The near miss with the bus left him rattled all the way home.
skill.analogy: Like a cup shaking on the table when a truck goes past.
skill.insteadOf: She became nervous and disturbed suddenly.

meaning: Momentarily flustered, shaken, or unnerved by an unexpected confrontation or crisis.
contrast: Not paralyzed terror; it is a temporary loss of composure under sudden sharp friction.
example: She was visibly rattled when the client aggressively challenged our financial projections in front of the board.

skill.work: The team was indignant when another group took credit for their work.
skill.everyday: She was indignant when the shopkeeper served people who came after her.
skill.analogy: Like a batsman given out off a no-ball: the anger is about fairness.
skill.insteadOf: They were angry because it was not fair.

meaning: Feeling or showing justifiable anger provoked by unfair treatment or injustice.
contrast: Not petty annoyance; indignation is rooted in a violation of shared principles or equity.
example: The team was indignant when management took credit for the open-source library they built over weekends.

skill.work: Despite pushback, Fatima stayed resolute about fixing the old code first.
skill.everyday: He was resolute about his morning walk, rain or shine.
skill.analogy: Like a train on its track: it doesn't swerve for every noise.
skill.insteadOf: She was very firm and didn't change her mind.

meaning: Admirably purposeful, determined, and unwavering in commitment.
contrast: Not blind stubbornness; resolute conviction comes from grounded clarity of purpose.
example: Despite intense pushback from legacy stakeholders, she remained resolute about retiring the monolithic codebase.

skill.work: With three deadlines this week, I'm a bit overwhelmed — can we prioritise?
skill.everyday: Cooking for twenty guests alone, Mum felt overwhelmed.
skill.analogy: Like a juggler handed one ball too many.
skill.insteadOf: I have so much work, I'm very tense.

meaning: Completely submerged by an excessive volume of demands, sensations, or tasks.
contrast: Deeper than simply being busy; cognitive processing capacity is maxed out and triage is needed.
example: Handling three production outages while fielding nonstop Slack pings left the on-call engineer completely overwhelmed.

skill.work: After cracking the bug, the whole team felt invigorated.
skill.everyday: A swim in the sea left me invigorated for the whole day.
skill.analogy: Like the first sip of strong filter coffee on a sleepy morning.
skill.insteadOf: I felt fresh and full of energy.

meaning: Filled with renewed energy, enthusiasm, and vitality.
contrast: Not frantic hyperactivity; it is a clean, focused surge of renewed motivation after a breakthrough.
example: Cracking the zero-copy buffer architecture left the whole systems team feeling invigorated.

skill.work: In the vendor meeting, his answers about the timeline were guarded.
skill.everyday: She's guarded with new neighbours until she knows them well.
skill.analogy: Like a batsman playing safe defensive shots, giving nothing away.
skill.insteadOf: He was not telling everything openly.

meaning: Cautious, reserved, and deliberately withholding vulnerability in conversation.
contrast: Different from shyness; guardedness is a conscious defensive posture to protect leverage or security.
example: During vendor contract negotiations, his answers regarding our fallback timeline were polite but strictly guarded.

skill.work: After his idea was rejected, he sat through stand-up in sullen silence.
skill.everyday: The kids were sullen all evening after the TV was switched off.
skill.analogy: Like a grey monsoon sky that won't rain and won't clear.
skill.insteadOf: He was angry and not talking to anyone.

meaning: Bad-tempered, gloomy, and silently resentful.
contrast: Beyond quietness; sullen silence radiates passive resistance and unresolved friction.
example: After his architectural proposal was rejected by the committee, he sat through the rest of the sprint sync in sullen silence.

skill.work: While everyone panicked over the bug, Joseph stayed nonchalant and fixed it.
skill.everyday: He was nonchalant about missing the bus — another comes in five minutes.
skill.analogy: Like a seasoned auto driver gliding through a jam without honking once.
skill.insteadOf: He was very cool and relaxed, no tension.

meaning: Appearing calm, casual, and completely unconcerned under pressure.
contrast: Not genuine negligence; nonchalance is often a deliberate display of unruffled executive ease.
example: While the rest of the room panicked over the broken build, the principal architect remained nonchalant as he drafted the hotfix.

skill.work: I was annoyed with myself when the typo turned out to be mine.
skill.everyday: He was embarrassed when his "shortcut" added half an hour to the trip.
skill.analogy: Like dropping a catch you loudly called for.
skill.insteadOf: I was chagrined to find the typo was mine.

meaning: Distressed, irritated, or embarrassed by failure or humiliation.
contrast: You'll mostly see it in writing. In speech, most people say "embarrassed" or "annoyed with myself".
example: She was chagrined to find the broken link came from her own change.

skill.work: I was mortified when I shared the wrong screen in the client demo.
skill.everyday: She was mortified when her phone rang in the quietest part of the film.
skill.analogy: Like tripping on stage at the annual function, in front of everyone.
skill.insteadOf: I felt very, very ashamed and bad.

meaning: Extremely embarrassed, humiliated, or ashamed.
contrast: Far stronger than mild awkwardness; it feels like wishing the ground would swallow you whole.
example: He was mortified when he shared the wrong screen during an all-hands presentation.

skill.work: We were exhilarated when the app crossed a million downloads.
skill.everyday: The first rollercoaster ride left my nephew exhilarated.
skill.analogy: Like the stadium the moment India hits the winning six.
skill.insteadOf: I was very, very happy and excited.

meaning: Filled with thrilling, energized joy and high spirits.
contrast: Higher octane than mild satisfaction; it is the physical rush of a hard-won high-stakes victory.
example: Watching our app hit number one on the App Store charts left the founders feeling exhilarated.

skill.work: He looked really disappointed when his feature was cut from the release.
skill.everyday: The kids' faces fell when the match was rained off.
skill.analogy: Like a kite soaring high, suddenly cut loose and falling.
skill.insteadOf: He looked crestfallen about the feature.

meaning: Sad, dejected, and visibly deflated after high expectations are suddenly dashed.
contrast: You'll mostly see it in writing. In speech, most people say "really disappointed" or "his face fell".
example: The intern looked crestfallen when his favourite feature was cut from the release.

skill.work: The client's silence after our proposal made me uneasy.
skill.everyday: Something felt off about the empty street at noon.
skill.analogy: Like a faint smell of gas in the kitchen that you can't trace.
skill.insteadOf: The client's silence left me disquieted.

meaning: Feeling an uneasy, subtle sense of worry, anxiety, or lurking danger.
contrast: You'll mostly see it in writing. In speech, most people say "uneasy" or "something felt off".
example: The sudden silence from the client following our pricing proposal left the account lead disquieted.

skill.work: The QA lead stayed defiant: no release without proper testing.
skill.everyday: The toddler gave a defiant 'No!' and kept the remote.
skill.analogy: Like a batsman who keeps hooking the bouncers he was told he can't play.
skill.insteadOf: She refused strongly and didn't listen to them.

meaning: Openly resisting, challenging, or refusing to comply with unjust authority.
contrast: Not reckless aggression; defiance is purposeful resistance against unfair constraints.
example: Despite executive pressure to ship untested code before the holiday, the QA lead took a defiant stance.

skill.work: He was remorseful after his script deleted a day of logs.
skill.everyday: She felt remorseful after snapping at her mother over nothing.
skill.analogy: Like replaying the shot that got you out, wishing you'd left it alone.
skill.insteadOf: He was feeling very sorry for what he did.

meaning: Filled with genuine, deep, and painful regret for having caused harm or error.
contrast: Deeper than saying sorry for politeness; remorse involves internal empathy and desire for restitution.
example: The developer was deeply remorseful after an unreviewed database script dropped three hours of customer audit logs.

skill.work: We were too eager to please the client, and the team got overloaded.
skill.everyday: He's so eager to please that he agrees to every plan his friends make.
skill.analogy: Like a waiter who says yes to every order, even ones the kitchen can't make.
skill.insteadOf: He's too complaisant with the client.

meaning: Willing to please others or comply with requests without challenge.
contrast: You'll mostly see it in writing. In speech, most people say "too eager to please"; it's also easy to mix up with "complacent".
example: The junior lead was too complaisant with the client's requests, and the team burned out.

skill.work: When the projector died mid-demo, he got flustered for a moment.
skill.everyday: The doorbell, the pressure cooker and the phone went off — I got flustered.
skill.analogy: Like a new cook when three pots boil over at once.
skill.insteadOf: I became confused and nervous suddenly.

meaning: Agitated, confused, and thrown off stride by sudden interruptions or unexpected pressure.
contrast: Not incompetence; it is a temporary scatter of focus when multiple things happen at once.
example: When the projector disconnected in the middle of his demo, he became momentarily flustered.

skill.work: After two hours of going in circles, the team got restless.
skill.everyday: The kids got impatient in the long queue at the fair.
skill.analogy: Like passengers on a train stopped outside the station for an hour.
skill.insteadOf: After two hours, the team grew restive.

meaning: Unable to remain still or silent; becoming impatient and difficult to control under restraint.
contrast: You'll mostly see it in writing. In speech, most people say "restless" or "getting impatient".
example: After two hours of debate with no decisions, the team grew restive.

skill.work: He looked smug when his prediction about the outage came true.
skill.everyday: My brother was smug all week after his team won.
skill.analogy: Like a neighbour who keeps reminding you he said it would rain.
skill.insteadOf: He was showing off too much about being right.

meaning: Having or showing an excessive, annoying pride in one’s achievements or correct guesses.
contrast: Different from humble satisfaction; smugness seeks validation by rubbing success in others’ faces.
example: He had a smug expression after his prediction about the cloud provider outage turned out to be exactly right.

skill.work: I felt humbled working alongside such experienced engineers.
skill.everyday: Losing to my ten-year-old niece at chess left me humbled.
skill.analogy: Like a club cricketer facing a Test bowler: you see how much is left to learn.
skill.insteadOf: I realised I don't know much.

meaning: Feeling modest, small, and profoundly aware of one’s limitations after witnessing greatness or experiencing a setback.
contrast: Not humiliation; being humbled is a healthy, grounded calibration of ego that fuels real learning.
example: Pair-programming with the original compiler author was a deeply humbling experience for our senior engineers.

skill.work: She was tenacious and chased the vendor until the fix arrived.
skill.everyday: My tenacious aunt bargained until the vendor finally gave in.
skill.analogy: Like a dog with a bone: it just won't let go.
skill.insteadOf: She didn't give up, she kept trying and trying.

meaning: Holding fast; persistent, stubborn in pursuing a goal despite intense difficulty.
contrast: Not mindless rigidity; tenacity is resilient grit that keeps trying new angles until the problem cracks.
example: Her tenacious debugging over four days finally tracked the memory corruption to an obscure third-party C library.

skill.work: After six weeks of weekend releases, the team was weary.
skill.everyday: After the long train journey, we were too weary to unpack.
skill.analogy: Like a bullock after ploughing all day: still standing, but slow.
skill.insteadOf: We were very tired from all this.

meaning: Feeling exhausted in strength, patience, or endurance after sustained friction.
contrast: Deeper than physical sleepiness; weariness is mental and emotional fatigue from prolonged uphill struggles.
example: The team was weary after six consecutive weeks of emergency weekend deployments.

skill.work: The manager kept a straight face while the vendor listed their demands.
skill.everyday: The ticket clerk showed nothing as the queue complained.
skill.analogy: Like a stone statue in the rain: things hit it, nothing shows.
skill.insteadOf: The manager stayed impassive.

meaning: Giving no sign of feeling or emotion; expressionless and calm.
contrast: You'll mostly see it in writing. In speech, most people say "kept a straight face" or "showed nothing".
example: The VP remained completely impassive as the vendor laid out their demands.

skill.work: He got a bit sulky when asked to follow the coding guidelines.
skill.everyday: The boy sulked because his brother got the window seat.
skill.analogy: Like a child stamping its feet because the ice cream is the wrong flavour.
skill.insteadOf: He gave a petulant reply.

meaning: Childishly sulky, bad-tempered, or peevish over trivial setbacks.
contrast: You'll mostly see it in writing. In speech, most people say "sulky" or "a bit childish".
example: He gave a petulant reply when asked to follow the team's formatting rules.

skill.work: I was really nervous walking up to present to the whole company.
skill.everyday: He was a bit scared before his first solo ride on the highway.
skill.analogy: Like a first-time diver standing at the edge of the board.
skill.insteadOf: I felt trepidatious before the talk.

meaning: Apprehensive and nervous with trembling anticipation before a high-stakes moment.
contrast: You'll mostly see it in writing. In speech, most people say "really nervous" or "a bit scared".
example: She felt trepidatious as she walked on stage to present the plan to the whole company.

skill.work: During the outage call, the incident lead's voice stayed serene.
skill.everyday: Sitting by the lake at sunrise, she felt serene.
skill.analogy: Like a still lake in the morning, before any boat goes out.
skill.insteadOf: She was very calm and peaceful.

meaning: Calm, peaceful, and untroubled by surrounding noise or chaotic urgency.
contrast: Not passive detachment; serenity is centered poise that allows clear thinking amid turbulence.
example: In the middle of the frantic outage escalation, the incident commander maintained a remarkably serene tone.

skill.work: The team was gleeful when a two-line fix made the page ten times faster.
skill.everyday: The kids were gleeful when school was cancelled for rain.
skill.analogy: Like a child who finds an extra laddoo in the box.
skill.insteadOf: They were very happy, jumping with joy.

meaning: Exuberantly or triumphantly joyful.
contrast: More playful and effervescent than quiet satisfaction; it feels like childhood delight at an unexpected win.
example: The engineers were gleeful when their tiny two-line regex optimization sped up the ingest pipeline tenfold.

skill.work: She was distraught when a week of her work was lost in a crash.
skill.everyday: He was distraught when his dog went missing.
skill.analogy: Like someone searching a crowded station for a lost child.
skill.insteadOf: She was very, very upset and crying.

meaning: Deeply agitated, heartbroken, and unable to think clearly due to grief or catastrophe.
contrast: Far beyond everyday worry; distraught states represent acute emotional crisis requiring support.
example: He was distraught when his only copy of the project files was lost in a laptop crash.

skill.work: Her kickoff was full of energy and lifted the team after a tough quarter.
skill.everyday: Our bubbly uncle had the whole wedding dancing.
skill.analogy: Like milk boiling over: energy that can't stay in the pot.
skill.insteadOf: Her ebullient kickoff lifted the team.

meaning: Cheerful, full of energy, and overflowing with enthusiastic warmth.
contrast: You'll mostly see it in writing. In speech, most people say "full of energy" or "bubbly".
example: Her ebullient kickoff talk lifted the team after a tough quarter.

skill.work: The PM was disconcerted when users didn't understand the main feature.
skill.everyday: I was disconcerted to find a stranger in my reserved seat.
skill.analogy: Like reaching for a stair that isn't there in the dark.
skill.insteadOf: I was confused and a bit disturbed.

meaning: Unsettled, confused, and thrown off balance by something unexpected.
contrast: Not sheer terror; it is the awkward psychological stumble when reality clashes with expectations.
example: The product manager was disconcerted when user interviews revealed that nobody understood the flagship feature.

skill.work: After the team moved floors, the old office looked empty and sad.
skill.everyday: A lonely little puppy waited outside the shop in the rain.
skill.analogy: Like the last chair left out after the wedding tent is packed away.
skill.insteadOf: The old office looked forlorn.

meaning: Pitifully sad, abandoned, or lonely in appearance or mood.
contrast: You'll mostly see it in writing. In speech, most people say "sad and lonely" or "deserted".
example: The old office floor looked forlorn after the whole team moved out.

skill.work: After winning the contract, she was gracious about the rival agency's work.
skill.everyday: After winning the carrom final, Grandpa was generous and praised his opponent.
skill.analogy: Like a captain who shakes every losing player's hand first.
skill.insteadOf: She was magnanimous about the rival agency.

meaning: Generous or forgiving, especially toward a rival or less powerful person.
contrast: You'll mostly see it in writing. In speech, most people say "gracious" or "generous" towards a rival.
example: After winning the contract, she was magnanimous in praising the rival agency's work.

skill.work: We were vexed by a bug that only appeared on Tuesdays.
skill.everyday: He was vexed by a crossword clue all through breakfast.
skill.analogy: Like a stone in your shoe that you can't find.
skill.insteadOf: This problem is irritating me a lot.

meaning: Frustrated, annoyed, and intellectually baffled by a recurring tricky problem.
contrast: Not explosive rage; vexation is the persistent mental itch of a puzzle that resists clean resolution.
example: The architects spent three weeks vexed by a nondeterministic race condition in the messaging queue.

skill.work: He made a passionate case for protecting user privacy.
skill.everyday: She's a huge, passionate fan of her local football club.
skill.analogy: Like a stadium crowd still singing for its team in the rain.
skill.insteadOf: He made a fervent case for privacy.

meaning: Having or displaying a passionate, sincere, and burning intensity of belief.
contrast: You'll mostly see it in writing. In speech, most people say "passionate".
example: He gave a fervent defence of user privacy in the product meeting.

skill.work: After four rebrands in five years, the senior staff were jaded.
skill.everyday: He's jaded about New Year resolutions after breaking every one.
skill.analogy: Like a tenth plate of the same biryani: nothing wrong, but no joy left.
skill.insteadOf: They were bored and didn't believe in it anymore.

meaning: Cynical, tired, or unenthusiastic after having had too much of something.
contrast: Different from laziness; jadedness is the defense mechanism of experienced veterans who have seen too many fads.
example: Having survived four corporate re-brandings in five years, the senior staff were understandably jaded.

skill.work: Even under tough questions, the spokesperson stayed calm.
skill.everyday: Our easy-going old cat sleeps through the Diwali crackers.
skill.analogy: Like a buffalo in a pond, unbothered by the traffic on the road.
skill.insteadOf: The spokesperson stayed placid.

meaning: Not easily upset or excited; calm, peaceful, and steady.
contrast: You'll mostly see it in writing. In speech, most people say "calm" or "easy-going".
example: Even under tough questions from reporters, the spokesperson remained placid.

skill.work: He stayed stoic through the restructuring and focused on his team.
skill.everyday: Grandma stayed stoic through the long power cut in May.
skill.analogy: Like a fielder who takes a hard ball on the shin and doesn't rub it.
skill.insteadOf: He didn't complain, he just tolerated it.

meaning: Enduring pain, stress, or hardship without showing feelings or complaining.
contrast: Not emotional death; stoicism is the disciplined mastery of one’s outward response to adversity.
example: He remained stoic throughout the grueling restructuring process, focusing entirely on supporting his team.

skill.work: The office was jubilant when the client signed.
skill.everyday: The whole street was jubilant after India won the final.
skill.analogy: Like the dressing room after a last-ball win.
skill.insteadOf: Everyone was very happy and celebrating.

meaning: Feeling or expressing great happiness, triumph, and celebration.
contrast: The peak collective roar of victory after an arduous team effort.
example: The engineering floor was jubilant the moment the Mars rover landing telemetry stream began rendering.

skill.work: I'm leery of vendors who promise zero downtime.
skill.everyday: After one bad experience, she's leery of online sellers.
skill.analogy: Like a cat that once touched a hot stove, now walking round the kitchen carefully.
skill.insteadOf: I don't trust them fully because of the past.

meaning: Cautious or wary due to realistic suspicions or past painful experiences.
contrast: Not irrational paranoia; being leery is prudent skepticism based on historical evidence.
example: Senior engineers were leery of the vendor’s claim of 100% automated schema migrations.

skill.work: The launch manager was up all night worrying, refreshing the dashboards.
skill.everyday: Mum was anxious until my late train finally arrived.
skill.analogy: Like checking the gas knob three times before leaving home.
skill.insteadOf: I spent a fretful night.

meaning: Feeling or expressing distress, irritation, and restless worry over details.
contrast: You'll mostly see it in writing. In speech, most people say "worried" or "anxious".
example: The launch manager spent a fretful night, refreshing the dashboards.

skill.work: The security scare galvanized the team into fixing every password.
skill.everyday: The flooding galvanized the whole colony into cleaning the drains.
skill.analogy: Like a wicket in the last over: the whole fielding side suddenly wakes up.
skill.insteadOf: It made everyone start working immediately.

meaning: Shocked, excited, or spurred into sudden, focused, and purposeful collective action.
contrast: More immediate and dynamic than vague inspiration; galvanization shocks a passive group into motion.
example: The security breach report galvanized the entire organization into implementing multi-factor authentication overnight.

skill.work: Clearing out her old desk, she felt a little wistful.
skill.everyday: Hearing the old Kishore Kumar song made Dad wistful.
skill.analogy: Like smiling at an old school photo, missing those days a little.
skill.insteadOf: I felt a little sad, remembering the old days.

meaning: Sad in a soft, thoughtful way about something lovely that is gone.
contrast: Not raw sadness; wistfulness holds warmth and longing together, like smiling at an old photo.
example: He felt wistful walking past his old college gate, hearing the same evening bell.

skill.work: Seeing the first version of our app made the founders nostalgic.
skill.everyday: The old Doordarshan theme music makes my parents nostalgic.
skill.analogy: Like opening Grandma's old tin trunk and finding your childhood toys.
skill.insteadOf: I remembered the old days and felt good.

meaning: Warmed by a memory of the past, wishing a piece of it back.
contrast: Not homesickness for a place; nostalgia can strike for a time, a song, or a smell.
example: The smell of rain on dry earth made her nostalgic for childhood monsoons.

skill.work: He looked sheepish when he realised he'd been on mute.
skill.everyday: She gave a sheepish grin after forgetting the milk again.
skill.analogy: Like a kid caught with a hand in the sweet box, smiling to be forgiven.
skill.insteadOf: He felt a little embarrassed and smiled.

meaning: Embarrassed with a small guilty smile, hoping to be forgiven fast.
contrast: Not deep shame; sheepishness admits a small silly mistake and asks for a laugh, not punishment.
example: He looked sheepish when the meeting realised he had been on mute for ten minutes.

skill.work: I always feel jittery before presenting to the leadership team.
skill.everyday: Two cups of strong coffee left me jittery all afternoon.
skill.analogy: Like a phone on vibrate that keeps buzzing on the table.
skill.insteadOf: I'm feeling very nervous and shaky.

meaning: Nervous energy buzzing in the body, shaky and over-alert.
contrast: Not calm worry; jitteriness is physical — tapping feet, fast pulse, too much coffee.
example: Three coffees before the demo left him jittery through every question.

skill.work: After six interviews in a row, I'm completely drained.
skill.everyday: After the wedding week, we were too drained to cook.
skill.analogy: Like a phone at 1% that won't charge.
skill.insteadOf: I am fully tired, no energy left.

meaning: Empty of all energy, with nothing left to give anyone.
contrast: Not sleepy-tired; drained means the tank reads zero even after sitting still.
example: After back-to-back interviews all day, she felt too drained to cook.

skill.work: After the late launch, I was wired till 2 a.m.
skill.everyday: The kids were wired after all the birthday cake.
skill.analogy: Like a fan on full speed that won't switch off.
skill.insteadOf: I am tired, but I can't sleep at all.

meaning: Buzzing with tense energy that will not switch off.
contrast: Not healthy energy; wired is overstimulated — alert but unable to rest.
example: He felt wired till 2 AM after the launch, replaying every alert.

skill.work: After the big launch, the team felt a bit flat for a week.
skill.everyday: The week after Diwali always feels flat.
skill.analogy: Like a cola left open overnight: nothing wrong, just no fizz.
skill.insteadOf: I'm not sad, but I'm not feeling anything good.

meaning: Low and dull, with no highs and no real lows either.
contrast: Not sharp sadness; flat is the absence of spark — food, jokes, and news all land the same.
example: The week after the festival, everything felt flat and grey.

skill.work: After three years on the same project, I've got itchy feet.
skill.everyday: Every summer, Riya gets itchy feet and plans a trip.
skill.analogy: Like a train passenger eyeing every station, wanting to get off somewhere new.
skill.insteadOf: I want some change, I'm bored of staying here.

meaning: Restless for a change of place or scene, unable to settle where you are.
contrast: Not boredom; itchy feet want a specific change — a trip, a move, a new start.
example: Two years in the same city gave him itchy feet, so he applied for the transfer.

skill.work: Sorry I was grumpy in stand-up — I'd skipped breakfast.
skill.everyday: Grandpa gets grumpy when the newspaper arrives late.
skill.analogy: Like an old ceiling fan that creaks with every turn.
skill.insteadOf: I was in a bad mood and irritated.

meaning: Irritable in a low, complaining way over small things.
contrast: Not real anger; grumpiness snaps about the toast and the traffic, never the real issue.
example: Skipping breakfast made him grumpy through the whole standup.

skill.work: He's been touchy about feedback since the tough review.
skill.everyday: She's touchy about her cooking, so praise the dal first.
skill.analogy: Like a sore tooth: even a light touch makes you flinch.
skill.insteadOf: He takes everything very personally these days.

meaning: Easily offended, reading sting into innocent remarks.
contrast: Not sensitivity, which feels deeply; touchiness reacts fast and takes things personally.
example: He was touchy about feedback all week after the bad review.

skill.work: Everyone was edgy during release week, jumping at every alert.
skill.everyday: Waiting for his exam results, my brother was edgy all day.
skill.analogy: Like a dog at the window, waiting for the doorbell.
skill.insteadOf: Everyone was tense and getting irritated quickly.

meaning: On edge, tense and ready to snap at small triggers.
contrast: Not fear; edginess is stretched nerves — fine now, but one ping away from snapping.
example: The team felt edgy all release week, flinching at every alert.

skill.work: She gets prickly when anyone asks about the delayed launch.
skill.everyday: He turns prickly whenever relatives ask about his plans.
skill.analogy: Like a cactus: fine to look at, painful to touch.
skill.insteadOf: She becomes angry when we ask about it.

meaning: Defensive and sharp, bristling at questions that feel like attacks.
contrast: Not rudeness for fun; prickliness guards a sore spot and warns people off it.
example: She turned prickly whenever anyone asked about the delayed launch.

skill.work: Let's break for lunch before the whole team gets hangry.
skill.everyday: Feed him first — he gets hangry by one o'clock.
skill.analogy: Like a phone that turns slow and cranky at low battery; food is the charger.
skill.insteadOf: I am angry because I am very hungry.

meaning: Angry because hungry — irritability that food fixes in minutes.
contrast: Not real anger at anyone; hangriness evaporates with the first few bites.
example: Miss lunch and I get hangry enough to snap at the calendar invite.

skill.work: Three client calls and a demo left me frazzled by noon.
skill.everyday: Cooking, homework and the doorbell — she was frazzled by seven.
skill.analogy: Like a rope fraying at the end, threads pulling in ten directions.
skill.insteadOf: I was totally disturbed doing many things at once.

meaning: Worn out and scattered by juggling too many things at once.
contrast: Not single-task tiredness; frazzled comes from split attention across ten open loops.
example: Cooking, calls, and the doorbell left her completely frazzled by noon.

skill.work: When the project was cancelled, I just felt numb for a day.
skill.everyday: After the shock of the break-in, she felt numb all evening.
skill.analogy: Like your hand after holding ice: you know it's there, but feel nothing.
skill.insteadOf: I didn't feel anything, I was blank.

meaning: Feeling nothing at all where something should hurt.
contrast: Not calm acceptance; numbness is the feeling switched off entirely, often right after shock.
example: Hearing the news, he felt numb all evening and just kept scrolling.

skill.work: The failed launch still feels raw, so let's give the team a few days.
skill.everyday: The break-up was still raw, so her friends kept things light.
skill.analogy: Like a fresh scrape on your knee: even a soft cloth stings.
skill.insteadOf: I am still very hurt about it.

meaning: Emotionally exposed, where every small touch stings.
contrast: Not ordinary upset; rawness is skin-off sensitivity in the days after a real blow.
example: The week after his father passed, even kind words left him feeling raw.

skill.work: In my first month at the Pune office, I was really homesick.
skill.everyday: Living abroad, she gets homesick every Diwali.
skill.analogy: Like a passenger watching every train going the other way, back home.
skill.insteadOf: I am missing my home and family very much.

meaning: Aching for home — its food, voices, and familiar corners.
contrast: Not general loneliness; homesickness points at one place and wants to go back to it.
example: Hostel food made him homesick for his mother's dal by week two.

skill.work: I feel self-conscious when I'm the first to speak on client calls.
skill.everyday: He felt self-conscious dancing at his cousin's wedding.
skill.analogy: Like being on the big screen at a cricket ground when the camera finds you.
skill.insteadOf: I feel shy, like everyone is looking at me.

meaning: Painfully aware of being watched, and sure you look wrong.
contrast: Not shyness about people; self-consciousness is about yourself under imagined inspection.
example: Speaking first in the big meeting made her self-conscious.

skill.work: The video call felt awkward when nobody unmuted to answer.
skill.everyday: It was awkward when I waved back at someone waving at someone else.
skill.analogy: Like two people at a doorway both stepping the same way, again and again.
skill.insteadOf: It was a very uncomfortable situation.

meaning: Socially clumsy and out of sync, unsure where to stand or what to say.
contrast: Not shame about a mistake; awkwardness is friction — the conversation just will not flow.
example: Alone with the client's CEO in the lift, the silence felt awkward.

skill.work: After the reorg, I felt adrift without a clear project.
skill.everyday: Between college and his first job, he felt adrift for months.
skill.analogy: Like a boat whose rope has slipped off the jetty.
skill.insteadOf: I had no direction, I was just passing time.

meaning: Floating without direction, unattached to any plan or purpose.
contrast: Not relaxing freedom; adrift feels like no anchor — free but uneasy about it.
example: Between jobs, he felt adrift for weeks before the routine returned.

skill.work: My last day with my old team felt bittersweet.
skill.everyday: Dropping my sister at her new college was bittersweet.
skill.analogy: Like karela cooked with jaggery: bitter and sweet in the same bite.
skill.insteadOf: I felt happy and sad, both.

meaning: Happy and sad at once about the same thing.
contrast: Not confusion; bittersweetness holds both feelings clearly — pride and loss side by side.
example: Her farewell party felt bittersweet — loved, and already missing everyone.

skill.work: I was relieved when the client approved the new date.
skill.everyday: We were relieved when the delayed flight finally landed.
skill.analogy: Like putting down a heavy shopping bag after climbing four floors.
skill.insteadOf: My tension went away.

meaning: The weight lifting off your chest when feared news turns out fine.
contrast: Not joy about gaining something; relief is joy about escaping something.
example: Hearing the tests were negative, the whole family felt relieved.

skill.work: With the release out and my inbox clear, I felt content.
skill.everyday: Sunday lunch, rain outside, a good book — I was content.
skill.analogy: Like the quiet after a good meal, when you want nothing more.
skill.insteadOf: I was happy, everything was fine.

meaning: Quietly satisfied, wanting nothing more than this moment.
contrast: Not excited happiness; contentment is still and full — no urge to post or chase.
example: Sunday lunch done, rain outside, he felt completely content.

skill.work: I'm grateful to Arjun for staying late to help me debug.
skill.everyday: We're grateful to the neighbours who fed our cat all week.
skill.analogy: Like someone saving you a seat on a packed train.
skill.insteadOf: Thank you so much, I am very thankful to you.

meaning: Warmly aware that someone's effort made your life easier.
contrast: Not generic happiness; gratitude points at a giver and wants to return the favour.
example: She felt grateful when her senior stayed back to debug with her.

skill.work: I'm proud of how the team handled the outage.
skill.everyday: He felt proud watching his daughter in her first school play.
skill.analogy: Like a parent clapping loudest at the annual function.
skill.insteadOf: I felt very good about my team.

meaning: Glowing with earned satisfaction about yourself or your people.
contrast: Not arrogance, which looks down; pride stands tall because of real effort behind it.
example: Watching his daughter hold the trophy, he felt fiercely proud.

skill.work: After finally sending the tough email, I felt light.
skill.everyday: After we cleared the air, I felt light all the way home.
skill.analogy: Like taking off a heavy backpack after a long trek.
skill.insteadOf: I felt free, no tension now.

meaning: Unburdened and easy, as if a weight quietly slid off.
contrast: Not excitement; lightness is the absence of dread — walking home after the apology.
example: After submitting the resignation, she felt lighter all the way home.

skill.work: After Arjun's farewell, the team room felt heavy all afternoon.
skill.everyday: The house felt heavy for days after Grandpa moved away.
skill.analogy: Like humid air before a storm, pressing on your chest.
skill.insteadOf: I was feeling sad and low.

meaning: Weighed down inside, as if the air itself got thicker.
contrast: Not sharp grief; heaviness is a dull pressure that sits on the chest for days.
example: The house felt heavy for days after Dadi's room went quiet.

skill.work: Same role for three years — I'm starting to feel stuck.
skill.everyday: Living in the same small town, she felt stuck.
skill.analogy: Like a car spinning its wheels in mud: engine roaring, going nowhere.
skill.insteadOf: Nothing is changing for me, I'm not growing.

meaning: Trapped in place while life visibly moves past you.
contrast: Not laziness; stuck is effort with no motion — pushing a door marked pull.
example: Same role, same desk, third year: he felt stuck watching juniors move ahead.

skill.work: When my manager named the exact problem I was facing, I felt seen.
skill.everyday: My friend remembered my exam date and called — I felt seen.
skill.analogy: Like a teacher who notices the quiet kid at the back of the class.
skill.insteadOf: I felt someone finally understood me.

meaning: Deeply understood by someone, perhaps for the first time.
contrast: Not praised for output; feeling seen is recognised for who you are underneath it.
example: When the manager named her exact struggle, she finally felt seen.

skill.work: My ideas were ignored in three meetings — I felt invisible.
skill.everyday: At the big family dinner, she felt invisible at the end of the table.
skill.analogy: Like a waiter walking past your raised hand again and again.
skill.insteadOf: Nobody is noticing me or my work.

meaning: Present but unnoticed, as if the room looks straight through you.
contrast: Not chosen solitude; invisibility is being overlooked where you hoped to matter.
example: Three ideas ignored in one meeting left him feeling invisible.
